candidate: Oral adenosine triphosphate (ATP), including ATP disodium/Peak ATP supplement formulations
disposition: Retain as a supplementary muscle-performance challenger; do not promote to a Track 2 nominee.
route: Nonspecific muscle-output or exercise-recovery compensation; no BUBR1-restoration route established.

study_evidence.design: 12-week randomized, double-blind, diet-controlled parallel comparison within a periodized resistance-training program; three training sessions weekly, followed by an overreaching phase and taper.
study_evidence.population: 24 resistance-trained young men entered the reported ATP/placebo comparison; 21 were analyzed (11 ATP, 10 placebo).
study_evidence.preparation: 400 mg/day ATP disodium (Peak ATP; supplier TSI) or maltodextrin placebo.

reported_results.total_1RM_strength_change: 55.3 ± 6.0 kg ATP versus 22.4 ± 7.1 kg placebo; group-by-time P < .001
reported_results.vertical_jump_power_change: 796 ± 75 W ATP versus 614 ± 52 W placebo; group-by-time P < .001
reported_results.quadriceps_thickness_change: 4.9 ± 1.0 mm ATP versus 2.5 ± 0.6 mm placebo; group-by-time P < .02
reported_results.lean_body_mass: 4.0 ± 0.4 kg ATP versus 2.1 ± 0.5 kg placebo over 12 weeks; reported group-by-time P < .009

limitations: Small, highly trained young male cohort; unusually intensive training included planned overreaching.
Multiple outcomes and timepoints; no multiplicity adjustment was identified in the scientific main.
Product/manufacturer and sponsor relationships were disclosed.
This is one study program with companion HMB and HMB-plus-ATP publications, not three independent ATP replications.

The current registry lists 44 actual participants and four interventions; the ATP paper reports its narrower ATP/placebo comparison. A 2017 published comment raised cross-paper protocol and denominator inconsistencies, and a published author response explained shared placebo participants and later-added controls. The response is not participant-level reanalysis, and no registry results are posted.

study_evidence.role: Oral bioavailability and systemic ATP counterevidence
study_evidence.design: A 28-day dose study in 32 healthy adults and a separate randomized crossover acute study in eight healthy adults.
study_evidence.preparation: Enteric-coated ATP at 250, 1,250 or 5,000 mg/day for 28 days; separately, a single 5,000 mg dose delivered using enteric-coated pellets or a nasoduodenal tube.
study_evidence.reported_results: No increase in whole-blood or plasma ATP was detected. Uric acid increased after high-dose/proximal-release exposure.
study_evidence.interpretation: This challenges a simple intact-ATP-to-muscle-energy explanation. It does not rule out local or metabolite-mediated effects, including purinergic signaling.

study_evidence.design: 14-day randomized double-blind study in 27 healthy men using 150 mg, 225 mg enteric-coated ATP, or placebo.
study_evidence.reported_results: No between-group effect on circulating ATP or muscle-strength parameters; selected within-group changes occurred in the high-dose arm.
limitations: Within-group change is not a treatment-versus-placebo effect.

study_evidence.design: 16-person randomized crossover; 400 mg/day ATP versus placebo for 15 days, followed by exhaustive repeated knee-extension testing.
study_evidence.registered_primary_outcome: Work performed across three fatigue tests.
study_evidence.reported_results: The paper reports no treatment benefit for total work, average power, high peak torque or work fatigue. Low peak torque in set 2 was 67.2 versus 62.3 Nm (P < .01); set-3 torque fatigue was a trend (P < .10).
study_evidence.registry_context: The current registry lists four interventions (placebo, ATP 250, ATP 400, ATP 400 plus a proprietary blend), actual enrollment 16, and no posted results. The article reports the ATP-400/placebo comparison.
limitations: The positive torque finding is a set-specific secondary result; the registered total-work primary outcome was not positive.
Industry funding and product-supplier relationships were disclosed.

study_evidence.design: PubMed abstract describes 244 participants randomized to oral ATP or placebo for four weeks after total knee arthroplasty.
study_evidence.reported_results: Abstract reports quadriceps-strength differences and lower pain/opioid use at postoperative days 7, 14, 21 and 28; numerical estimates and detailed endpoint hierarchy are not given in the abstract.
study_evidence.source_scope: Abstract only. The publisher full text was not accessible from the official journal source during this review; no detailed methods, figures, or full statistical analysis are claimed.
limitations: Surgical recovery and pain-management context; not a BUB1B or inherited myopathy study.
Short-term abstract result without effect estimates or complete methods.

study_evidence.design: Human uncontrolled pilot in 12 resistance-trained adults alongside a rat study.
study_evidence.reported_results: The human pilot reported blood-flow and brachial-dilation changes after 400 mg/day ATP over 12 weeks.
limitations: No placebo/control group in the human data.
Blood flow is not muscle strength, useful function, BUBR1 restoration, or chromosome fidelity.
Mechanism and source of the circulating signal remain unresolved.

publication_context.current_registry: 44 actual participants; four arms (placebo, HMB, ATP, ATP plus HMB); no results section posted.

comment_and_response.comment: Gentles and Phillips, 2017, PMCID PMC5496306, raised cross-publication protocol and participant-count questions.
comment_and_response.author_response: Wilson, 2017, PMCID PMC5704583, described shared placebo participants, later additional controls for the ATP analysis, and corrected sample-characteristic values.
comment_and_response.appraisal: The response provides a plausible study-accounting explanation, but the shared dataset must not be counted as independent replication; the public registry still contains no trial results or participant-level data.

competitiveness.versus_niacin: ATP has more direct controlled muscle-performance signals in exercise settings; niacin retains the more proximal NAD/SIRT2/BUBR1 hypothesis. Their endpoints and populations do not support a single efficacy ranking.
competitiveness.versus_apitegromab: ATP is an oral supplement route, but lacks apitegromab's randomized pediatric neuromuscular-disease motor-function evidence; neither is proven for MVA.
competitiveness.versus_creatine: The repository's creatine comparison includes controlled studies in neuromuscular and adult myopathy populations; ATP's evidence is narrower, partly abstract-only, and concentrated in healthy training or postoperative settings.
competitiveness.decision: Do not displace niacin or apitegromab, and do not add ATP to the pitch's primary nominees. Retain only as a low-cost supplementary functional benchmark if space allows.

promotion_trigger: Independent, prospectively specified evidence with an authenticated ATP formulation and interpretable exposure, followed by a relevant affected/corrected muscle model showing greater absolute output without reduced renewal or worsened chromosome fidelity. Any BUBR1-restoration claim would require direct BUB1B/BUBR1 target and function measurements.
